summary:
Consensual sexual conduct between adults was decriminalised on 16 May 1991 under the Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act, and no source records a prosecution risk for a visitor on that basis. The criminal law retains an unequal age of consent: 16 years for opposite-sex acts and 18 years for same-sex acts, so a trans visitor in a relationship that local law reads as same-sex falls under the higher threshold.

Gender identity appears in no anti-discrimination or anti-harassment statute in the Bahamas. Discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, education, housing, healthcare, banking and public businesses is not illegal, and the same gap applies to sexual orientation. The Constitution's prohibition on discrimination covers neither characteristic. The 2006 Constitutional Reform Commission did not regard sexual orientation as deserving protection, and efforts to include it in a proposed Constitution were blocked by members citing religious opposition.

No national hate-crime law exists to prevent or punish violence directed at LGBT people, and discrimination in healthcare or education on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is not illegal.

Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United launched the 'Bahamian Trans Lives Matter' campaign in April 2016, stating that no laws protect transgender and intersex Bahamians and advocating, through member Torri Culmer, against job termination for trans and intersex workers.

Trans people have been named as targets by a serving official. Government member Leslie Miller publicly called for the "Exile of Transgender out of the Bahamas," urged financial contributions to relocate transgender people to a private island so that "they stay out of the way," and pledged $1,000 toward it. Former Prime Minister Perry Christie stated in 2013 that he did not believe in same-sex marriage and in 2016 that a referendum would not legalise it, defining marriage as between male and female determined at birth. The 2016 referendum bills were not inclusive of transgender or intersex people.

Marriage and civil unions are not available to same-sex couples. The Marriage Act defines marriage as between a man and a woman, and maritime marriage law provides that a marriage is void if contracted between two men or two women. In 2011 former Minister of State Zhivargo Laing stated that such a marriage is void, calling this a community standard. Same-sex households are denied the rights given to opposite-sex married couples.

Violence against gay and gender-nonconforming people has met with judicial tolerance. A defendant was acquitted in 2009 of murdering a gay HIV-positive man after invoking a "gay panic" defence; on 10 June 2010 the Court of Appeal president stated that "One is entitled to use whatever force is necessary to prevent one's self-being the victim of a homosexual act"; and an accused in the 2007 Harl Taylor slaying was found not guilty. Nine murders of gay men between 2001 and 2015 remain unsolved. That figure is a raw count over fourteen years with no population denominator supplied by the sources, so it supports no per-capita comparison.

A gay visitor was physically attacked during a tourist event. On 8 May 2017 The Tribune reported that Adrian Brown, 24, Jamaica-born and US-resident, was treated at Doctors Hospital for a head laceration after being targeted and beaten because he is gay at the Bahamas Junkanoo Carnival early that Saturday, and that he wants charges laid.

Police have moved against LGBT social space. On 6 October 2007 officers raided a gay party in downtown Nassau; no arrests were possible because no crime had been committed, guests demanded an apology, and the Ministry of Tourism issued one to the cruise company. LGBT tourist groups have also been protested: church group opposition to Rosie O'Donnell's 2004 cruise, a 1998 protest against a lesbian cruise, and in September 2007 the formation of an anti-gay committee by the Bahamas Christian Council over a request to a local cable company to carry the LGBTQ channel Logo.

No exclusively gay bars or clubs exist; the Nassau scene is underground, and LGBT groups are often pressured to keep social events hidden. Many Bahamians belong to conservative Christian denominations treating homosexuality and cross-dressing as decadence, and politicians have been leery of publicly supporting LGBT-rights legislation. Due to lack of confidence in the judicial system, legal inequalities and homophobia, many LGBT people keep sexual orientation or gender identity private.

There is no prohibition on LGBT citizens serving in the police, military or prison service, and in May 1998 National Security Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Frank Watson declared that those forces do not discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation.

No HIV-specific or trans-specific care provisions are recorded in the sources.
tangentialFactors:
National public-opinion surveys record strong opposition to LGBT visibility, though they measure attitudes rather than incidents and surveyed the general population, not trans respondents: 85.5% strongly disapproved of same-sex marriage in 2015 against 10.6% approving, and over 84% strongly disapproved of a gay or lesbian politician in 2013 with 12% positive. Both figures are now a decade or more old.

The Canadian government issued travel advice in 2016 warning gay couples about the risk of homophobia in the Bahamas, an external assessment that matches the domestic picture of official and church opposition.

Statutory protection that does exist is narrow. The Data Protection (Privacy of Personal Information) Act 2003 lists "sexual life" as sensitive personal data, and the Communications Act 2009 empowers URCA to issue codes of practice against content likely to incite hatred or vilify persons on the basis of sexual preference. Neither instrument addresses gender identity.

Censorship has been applied to LGBT content: the Plays and Films Control Board banned Brokeback Mountain in March 2006 and attempted to block a public-square screening of Children of God on 24 June 2011, an attempt the government overruled.

Social consequences for visibility have included the stripping of an 18-year-old beauty queen's crown in 2005 after she confirmed she was a lesbian.

The 1998 ministerial non-discrimination declaration covers sexual orientation only; no source extends it to gender identity, and the trans-specific record runs in the opposite direction through Leslie Miller's 2016-era call for exile.
localsOnly:
Residents have no statutory recourse against discrimination on the basis of gender identity or sexual orientation in employment, education, housing, healthcare, banking or public businesses. A clause banning sexual-orientation workplace discrimination in the 2001 Employment Bill was removed shortly after passage, and no comparable clause has since been enacted.

The Constitution's non-discrimination provision does not include gender identity or sexual orientation, and the 2006 reform process declined to add sexual orientation, with inclusion efforts blocked on religious grounds.

There are no national hate-crime laws protecting LGBT residents, and the nine unsolved murders of gay men recorded between 2001 and 2015 have produced no documented convictions in those cases.

Domestic advocacy is organised but small: Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United ran the 'Bahamian Trans Lives Matter' campaign from April 2016, focused on the absence of legal protection and on job termination facing trans and intersex workers.

LGBT residents keep sexual orientation or gender identity private because of lack of confidence in the judicial system, legal inequalities and homophobia, and local groups are often pressured to keep social events hidden; there are no exclusively gay bars or clubs.
